title: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
summary: Internal vs external fragmentation, size-class rounding, placement policy, page-pinning and purging in jemalloc and glibc, and how Redis, Mesh and the Linux kernel measure and fix fragmentation.
outcomes: Explain internal vs external fragmentation and compute fragmentation over live data for a heap
Compute the internal waste of a request under power-of-two and jemalloc size classes
Explain why address-ordered first fit and best fit fragment far less than next fit on real programs
Explain why a few live objects pin pages, and how decay-based purging returns the rest
Diagnose a fragmentation report by layer and choose between purging, defragmentation and compaction

lessons.title: Free memory you cannot use: two kinds of fragmentation

blocks.md:
Picture a cache service that holds about 8 GiB of live objects, day after day. Yet its resident memory climbs from 9 GiB to 14 GiB over a week until the container is killed for running out of memory. Nothing leaked: every object that was freed really was freed. The memory went to **fragmentation**, space the allocator holds but cannot use for the requests that arrive.

From the prerequisite course you know how allocators carve big regions into blocks using free lists, slabs and buddies. This course is about the waste those choices leave behind, how to measure it, and what real allocators and kernels do about it.

Mel Gorman's book on the Linux memory manager gives the two classic definitions:

- **External fragmentation** is the inability to service a request because the available memory exists only in small blocks. The free bytes are there, just not in one piece.
- **Internal fragmentation** is wasted space inside a block, where a large block had to be assigned to serve a small request.

Both make the footprint bigger than the live data. They have different causes, so they need different fixes.

blocks.title: External fragmentation in a 12 KiB heap

scenes.caption: Twelve 1 KiB objects a to l fill a 12 KiB heap. The two cells marked - are address space the heap has not grown into yet.
Every second object is freed. 6 KiB is now free, but it sits in six separate 1 KiB holes, each between two live objects, so no two holes can merge.
A 2 KiB request X arrives. 6 KiB is free, yet no hole is 2 KiB long. This is external fragmentation: free memory in pieces too small for the request.
The allocator must grow the heap to 14 KiB to place X. Live data is 8 KiB (six objects plus X), so 6 KiB of the footprint is fragmentation.

blocks.md: Internal fragmentation looks different. Suppose an allocator hands out only 1 KiB chunks and the program asks for 600 bytes. It gets a whole chunk, and the other 424 bytes are unusable by anyone until the object is freed: 41.4% of that chunk is waste. No free list shows it, because the allocator considers the chunk in use.

To compare allocators you need one number. Johnstone and Wilson's 1998 study expresses fragmentation as the memory the allocator uses *over and above* the live data, as a percentage of the live data. A perfect allocator scores 0%.

blocks.caption: The 12 KiB heap example after it grows. The ratio form, footprint / live = 1.75, is what tools like Redis report.

blocks.md: When you measure matters as much as what. The paper defines four measures on one memory-use trace: averaged over time, at the moment of peak live data, at the moment of peak footprint, and peak footprint against peak live data. For the GCC trace under a simple power-of-two allocator, the four give wildly different answers.

blocks.title: One trace, four fragmentation numbers (Johnstone and Wilson)

scenes.caption: GCC compiling one program with the simple segregated 2^N allocator. Same run, same allocator: 39.8% to 462% depending on where you look.
The paper reports measures #3 and #4. #4 (peak footprint against peak live, here 100%) answers the provisioning question: how much RAM must I buy?

blocks.md: Fragmentation is not a leak. In a leak, *live* data grows because the program forgets to free. With fragmentation, live data is flat while the *footprint* grows. Tell them apart by comparing the bytes the allocator says are allocated with the memory it holds: a leak raises both, fragmentation widens the gap.

Internal fragmentation is waste inside handed-out blocks (a rounding cost). External fragmentation is free memory split into holes too small to use (a placement and lifetime cost). Both are measured against live data, and the number depends on when you measure.

blocks.question: A service's allocator reports 2.0 GiB allocated to the application at every sample for a week, while resident memory rises from 2.4 GiB to 3.6 GiB. What is the best first hypothesis?
options: A memory leak in the application
Fragmentation: the gap between held and live memory is growing
The kernel is counting page cache as resident
Internal fragmentation from size classes, which grows over time
blocks.explain: Allocated bytes are flat, so live data is not growing: that rules out a leak. The growing gap is memory the allocator holds but cannot reuse or return. Size-class rounding is fixed per object, so it cannot grow while the same objects stay live.

blocks.question: A heap has 6 KiB free in six 1 KiB holes and gets a 2 KiB request. Which change would let the request succeed without growing the heap?
options: Rounding the request up to 4 KiB
Freeing one more object that sits between two holes, so they coalesce
Switching to a faster free-list search
Adding a second free list for 1 KiB holes
blocks.explain: The request fails because no two free bytes are adjacent. Freeing an object between two holes lets the allocator coalesce them into a 3 KiB hole. Search speed and extra lists do not create contiguity, and rounding up makes the request harder to fit.

lessons.title: Size classes: buying speed with internal waste

blocks.md:
Most modern allocators do not keep one free list of arbitrary blocks. They round every request up to a **size class** and keep separate storage per class (segregated free lists or slabs, from the prerequisite). Within one class every free slot fits every request, so allocation is a pop from a list with no searching and no splitting.

The price is rounding. If a 129-byte request is served from a 256-byte class, 127 bytes are internal fragmentation for the whole life of that object.

How much rounding costs depends on how closely the classes are spaced. With pure **powers of two**, a request just above $2^k$ gets a $2^{k+1}$ block, so almost half the block is waste. Johnstone and Wilson note that binary buddy systems, which round this way, usually have internal fragmentation of about 25%.

**jemalloc** spaces classes more finely. Its manual says classes are spaced so that there are four size classes for each doubling, which limits internal fragmentation to approximately 20% for all but the smallest classes. Between 128 and 256 bytes the classes are 160, 192, 224 and 256.

blocks.tex: w(x) = \frac{c(x) - x}{c(x)}, \quad c(x) = s\left\lceil \frac{x}{s} \right\rceil, \quad s = \frac{2^{k}}{n} \text{ for } 2^k < x \le 2^{k+1}
blocks.caption: Waste fraction w for a request of x bytes with n classes per doubling and spacing s. The worst request is 2^k + 1, giving w = (s - 1)/(s(n + 1)), just under 1/(n + 1).

blocks.title: Waste fraction vs request size, n classes per doubling

scenes.caption: n = 1 is pure powers of two: both curves coincide. Just above each power of two (129, 257, 513, 1025) almost 50% of the block is wasted.
n = 2 adds a class halfway (192, 384, 768, 1536). Worst case drops to about 33%.
n = 4 is jemalloc's spacing. The sawtooth peaks just under 20% (1,025 bytes gets 1,280: 19.9%), matching the manual's approximately 20%.
n = 8 halves the spacing again and caps waste near 11%. Finer classes cut rounding waste, but each class needs its own slabs and caches.

blocks.prompt: With jemalloc's classes (4 KiB pages, 16-byte quantum), a program calls `malloc(4097)`. How many bytes does it really get, and how many would a power-of-two allocator hand out?
blocks.reveal: jemalloc's next class above 4,096 is **5 KiB** (5,120 bytes), so 1,023 bytes (19.98% of the block) are wasted. A power-of-two allocator returns **8,192** bytes and wastes 4,095 (49.99%). One byte over a boundary costs a lot under either scheme, which is why it pays to know where the boundaries are.

blocks.title: Six objects: bytes requested vs bytes handed out

scenes.caption: Requested sizes: 2,250 bytes in total across six objects.
jemalloc classes: 112, 160, 224, 320, 640, 1024. Total 2,480 bytes, so 9.3% of the footprint is internal waste.
Power-of-two classes: 128, 256, 256, 512, 1024, 1024. Total 3,200 bytes, 29.7% waste. The 130 and 520 byte objects are the worst hit.

blocks.md: Finer classes are not free. Every class keeps its own slabs, and each class can have a partly filled slab at any moment, so more classes means more partly empty memory. Thread caches multiply this per thread: the jemalloc manual warns that thread-specific caching increases memory usage and fragmentation, since a bounded number of objects can remain allocated in each thread cache. Size-class design trades internal waste against this spread.

You can see and use the class boundaries:

- `malloc_usable_size(p)` returns the real size of the block, class rounding included.
- jemalloc's manual notes that `realloc` growth or shrinkage trivially succeeds in place when the old and new sizes round up to the same class.
- Hot structs just over a boundary are worth trimming. A 130-byte record lands in the 160 class; shaving it to 128 bytes moves it to the 128 class and saves 20% of the memory per object.

`sizeof` is not what you pay. With a million 130-byte records you might budget 124 MiB, but jemalloc hands out 160 bytes each (153 MiB) and a power-of-two allocator 256 (244 MiB). Measure with `malloc_usable_size` or allocator stats, not by multiplying `sizeof`.

blocks.question: Under jemalloc, which request wastes the largest fraction of its block?
options: 1,000 bytes
33 bytes
300 bytes
2,048 bytes
blocks.explain: 33 bytes rounds to the 48-byte class (16-byte spacing among small classes), wasting 31.25%. The manual's 20% bound holds for all but the smallest classes. 1,000 goes to 1,024 (2.3%), 300 to 320 (6.25%), and 2,048 is exactly a class (0%).

blocks.question: A team patches their allocator from 4 to 8 classes per doubling. Which outcome should they expect?
options: Total memory always falls by about 9%
External fragmentation disappears because rounding is smaller
Allocation becomes slower because each request must search all classes
Worst-case internal waste falls from about 20% to about 11%, with more partly empty slabs to offset part of the gain
blocks.explain: Worst-case waste is just under 1/(n+1): 20% for n = 4, 11% for n = 8. But twice as many classes means twice as many places for partly filled slabs and cached objects to sit, so the net saving depends on the workload. Class lookup stays a computation, not a search.

lessons.title: Placement policy: where a block goes decides what survives

blocks.md:
External fragmentation is decided at allocation time. When several free holes fit a request, the **placement policy** picks one:

- **First fit**: scan the free list from the start, take the first hole big enough.
- **Next fit**: like first fit, but resume the scan where the last one stopped (a roving pointer).
- **Best fit**: take the smallest hole that fits.

The order of the free list matters too: LIFO (most recently freed first), FIFO, or address-ordered (AO). After placing a block, the leftover part of the hole stays free, and freed blocks are **coalesced** with free neighbours.

blocks.title: First fit vs best fit on the same 16-cell heap

scenes.caption: Both heaps hold A (2 cells), B (5), C (1), D (2), E (6). Same contents, two policies.
B and D are freed. Each heap has a 5-cell hole at 2 and a 2-cell hole at 8: 7 free cells.
X needs 2 cells. First fit takes the first hole that fits, splitting the 5-hole. Best fit takes the exact 2-cell hole at 8 and leaves the big hole intact.
Y needs 5 cells. First fit has 5 free cells, but as holes of 3 and 2: it must grow the heap. Best fit puts Y in the untouched 5-hole and the heap stays 16 cells.

blocks.md: Do not over-learn this toy. A different request sequence can make best fit lose, and in theory every allocator that cannot move objects has bad cases. Robson's classic result, as summarised by the Mesh paper, is that the memory blow-up can reach the log of the ratio between the largest and smallest object sizes.

blocks.caption: Robson's worst case for a program that allocates 16-byte and 128 KiB objects: up to 13x the live memory, whatever placement policy is used.

blocks.md: So the real question is empirical: how do policies behave on real programs? Johnstone and Wilson traced every malloc, realloc and free of eight real C and C++ programs (including GCC, Ghostscript, Perl and Espresso), then replayed the traces through many policies. They removed header and alignment overheads so that only the policy itself was measured. Earlier studies had used synthetic random traces, which the authors argue do not predict behaviour on real programs.

blocks.prompt: Next fit was introduced as an "optimization" of first fit: by starting each search where the last ended, it avoids piling small leftover holes at the front of the list. Will it fragment less or more than address-ordered first fit on real programs?
blocks.reveal: **More, by a lot.** The paper says this "optimization" generally increases fragmentation. Averaged over the eight traces (measure #4), next fit LIFO wasted 38.4% while address-ordered first fit with 8K sbrk wasted 0.78% (2.30% without the 8K sbrk). Spreading allocations across the whole heap stops old free regions from resting long enough for their neighbours to die and coalesce with them.

scenes.caption: Johnstone and Wilson, Table 4: fragmentation over live memory, averaged over the eight programs. AO = address-ordered; 8K = heap grown in 8 KiB sbrk steps. Both are under 1%.

Same placement idea, different free-list order: first fit with a LIFO list jumps to 36.3%, and next fit LIFO to 38.4%. The paper singles out a disastrous result on Ghostscript (179% for first fit LIFO).
Binary buddy (53.4%) and simple segregated storage with power-of-two classes and no coalescing (73.6%) trade extra internal waste for less external fragmentation and pay for it.

blocks.md:
Why do the good policies win? The paper's answer: they all coalesce freed memory immediately, and they all prefer to reuse memory that was freed *recently* or that sits at one end of the heap. That leaves other free regions alone long enough for their neighbours to die too, so those regions merge into ever larger holes.

This works because programs are kind: objects allocated at about the same time tend to die at about the same time. On average across the traces, after just 32K of further allocation, 90% of freed bytes had both temporal neighbours (the objects allocated just before and after) free as well. Lea's allocator (dlmalloc 2.6.1, segregated fit) approximates best fit with fast per-size lists and scored 2.28%.

Separate policy from mechanism. Good policies (address-ordered first fit, best fit, segregated fit approximating best fit) gave near-zero fragmentation on real traces once implementation overheads were removed. The remaining job is to implement such a policy fast, which is what size-classed allocators do.

"Fragmentation is solved" is not the lesson. The study covers eight single-threaded C and C++ programs from the 1990s, and the authors call for more work on unusual program behaviour. Long-running servers with phase changes, many threads and per-thread caches are exactly that kind of workload, as the next lesson shows.

blocks.question: Which allocator change is most likely to raise fragmentation, based on Johnstone and Wilson's results?
options: Switching from best fit to address-ordered first fit
Switching from address-ordered first fit to next fit with a roving pointer
Coalescing freed blocks immediately
Using segregated free lists that approximate best fit
blocks.explain: Next fit spreads allocation over the whole heap, which interrupts the "let old regions rest and merge" effect. AO first fit and best fit (with 8K sbrk) were both under 1% on average, immediate coalescing is a shared trait of the good policies, and segregated fit (Lea) approximates best fit.

blocks.question: A program allocates objects from 16 bytes to 128 KiB. A colleague says Robson's bound proves it will use 13x its live memory. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; the bound applies to every program with that size range
Robson's bound only applies to garbage-collected languages
The bound is a worst case over adversarial sequences; real traces with good policies were near 0%
The bound is log base 10, so it is about 4x
blocks.explain: Robson's result says some request sequence can force that blow-up on any non-moving allocator. It does not say typical programs reach it. Johnstone and Wilson measured near-zero fragmentation for good policies on real programs.

lessons.title: Why freed memory does not go back: pages, arenas, purging

blocks.md:
A size-classed allocator can reuse a freed slot instantly for the same class. Giving memory back to the operating system is harder: the kernel works in pages, so a page can be returned only when **no live object at all** sits on it. One survivor pins the whole page.

The Redis docs describe the result: fill an instance with 5 GB of data, delete 2 GB, and resident memory will probably still be around 5 GB, because most removed keys were allocated on the same pages as keys that still exist.

blocks.prompt: Simplified model: 1 GiB of 64-byte objects, packed 64 per 4 KiB page (262,144 pages). The program frees 90% of the objects at random, keeping 102.4 MiB live. How much of the 1 GiB can be returned to the OS?
blocks.reveal: Almost none. A page is empty only if all 64 of its objects were freed: $0.9^{64} \approx 0.0012$. That is about 309 of 262,144 pages, so roughly **1,022.8 MiB stays resident** to hold 102.4 MiB of live data, a footprint 10x the live data. Real slabs may span several pages, which makes it even harder for one to empty.

blocks.title: 64 pages, live objects per page (64 slots each)

scenes.caption: 64 pages, each full with 64 live 64-byte objects: 4,096 objects.
90% of objects freed at random (simulated, seed 7): 409 live objects remain, but every page still holds between 2 and 13 of them. Zero pages can be returned.

If the same 409 objects could be moved, they would fill 7 pages (6 full plus 25 objects) and 57 pages could go back to the OS. C and C++ allocators cannot move objects, because pointers to them would break.

blocks.title: Fraction of pages that become empty

scenes.caption: With one object per page (k = 1), the empty fraction equals the freed fraction: memory returns as fast as it is freed.
k = 8 (512-byte objects): keeping 20% live already pins 83% of pages, since 1 minus 0.8^8 is 0.83.
k = 64: the curve hugs zero. Even at 5% live, only 3.8% of pages are empty, assuming objects die at random.
Simplified: real programs free objects in correlated batches (born together, die together), which empties pages far more often than random death does.

blocks.md:
Allocators differ in how they return memory:

- **glibc malloc** grows the main heap with `sbrk` and, per `mallopt(3)`, can trim it only when enough contiguous free memory sits at the **top** (`M_TRIM_THRESHOLD`, initially 128 KiB). A single live chunk near the top pins everything below it. Large requests, at least `M_MMAP_THRESHOLD` (initially 128 KiB, raised dynamically), get their own `mmap` and can always be returned independently. `malloc_trim` has, since glibc 2.8, released whole free pages in all arenas.
- **jemalloc** manages page-aligned extents and **purges** unused pages with calls like `madvise`, rather than only trimming from the top.

Concurrency adds more waste. To avoid lock contention, allocators keep several **arenas** that manage memory completely independently. jemalloc's default is four arenas per CPU, and its manual says this costs "a small fixed increase in overall memory fragmentation": a page freed in one arena cannot serve a request in another. **Thread caches** (tcache, by default up to 32 KiB classes) keep freed objects parked per thread. glibc's `M_ARENA_MAX` documents the same trade: more arenas, less contention, more memory.

blocks.title: Life of a jemalloc page after its last object is freed

scenes.caption: Live objects sit on active pages. stats.allocated counts their bytes; stats.active counts whole pages, so active minus allocated is the slack inside partly used pages.
When the last object on a page is freed, the page becomes dirty: unused but still resident, and still counted in RSS.
If a request arrives soon, a dirty page is reused with no system call and no page fault. Keeping dirty pages for a while is a speed choice.
Otherwise they decay: opt.dirty_decay_ms (default 10 s) sets roughly how long until a set of dirty pages is purged, along a sigmoidal curve.
With the default opt.muzzy_decay_ms of 0, dirty pages are purged straight to clean. If muzzy decay is enabled, they first become muzzy via MADV_FREE. RSS falls once pages are purged.

blocks.md:
jemalloc exposes each layer through `mallctl`. Read `stats.*` after bumping `epoch`, which refreshes the statistics:

- `stats.allocated`: bytes the application holds.
- `stats.active`: bytes in active pages (a multiple of the page size, at least `allocated`).
- `stats.resident`: physically resident pages, including unused dirty ones.
- `stats.retained`: virtual memory kept instead of unmapped, with no strong tie to physical memory.

blocks.caption: Requires jemalloc built with stats (the default). Two ratios separate fragmentation inside pages from unused pages waiting to be purged.

blocks.md: Setting `dirty_decay_ms` to 0 is not a free fix. The manual says it purges dirty pages immediately when they are created, so every page that empties pays for a purge, and every later reuse pays a page fault. It lowers RSS that is merely waiting; it does nothing for pages pinned by live objects.

blocks.question: A jemalloc process shows allocated 3.0 GiB, active 3.1 GiB, resident 5.0 GiB. What is most of the gap?
options: Pages pinned by a few live objects each
Internal fragmentation from size classes
Unused dirty pages that have not been purged yet
A memory leak
blocks.explain: active is only 0.1 GiB above allocated, so pages that hold objects are nearly full: little slack between objects (class rounding is already inside allocated and cannot be seen here). resident is 1.9 GiB above active, and resident includes unused dirty pages (plus metadata). That memory will drop as decay purges it, or can be purged explicitly.

blocks.question: In the 64-objects-per-page model, a workload frees 95% of its objects at random. What fraction of pages becomes returnable?
options: About 95%
About 3.8%
About 50%
Exactly 0%
blocks.explain: A page is empty only if all 64 objects died: 0.95^64 is about 0.0375, so about 3.8% of pages. The other 96% each hold at least one survivor and stay resident. Correlated lifetimes in real programs do better than this random model.

lessons.title: Measuring and fixing fragmentation in production

blocks.md: Diagnose fragmentation by splitting the gap between live data and RSS into layers, from the inside out: application bytes, bytes the allocator handed out, pages that hold objects, pages the allocator keeps resident, and everything else in the process. Redis reports exactly these layers in `INFO memory`, using jemalloc's statistics.

blocks.caption: When used equals allocated (the Redis docs say they are normally the same), the headline ratio factors into three causes.

blocks.md: The Redis docs say `allocator_frag_ratio` (active over allocated) is the true external fragmentation metric, not `mem_fragmentation_ratio`. `allocator_rss_ratio` usually shows pages the allocator can and probably will soon release. The headline ratio also counts code, shared libraries and stacks, so the docs add that a high ratio such as 1.5 means little when the absolute difference is only a few megabytes.

blocks.title: A Redis instance, layer by layer (illustrative numbers)

scenes.caption: The headline: 4.7 GiB RSS for 3.0 GiB of data, mem_fragmentation_ratio 1.57.
allocator_frag_ratio = 4.2 / 3.0 = 1.40: 1.2 GiB of slack inside pages that still hold objects. This is the external fragmentation.
allocator_rss_ratio = 4.6 / 4.2 = 1.10: 0.4 GiB of unused pages waiting to be purged. rss_overhead = 4.7 / 4.6 = 1.02: 0.1 GiB outside the heap.

blocks.prompt: In that instance, which action targets the biggest share of the 1.7 GiB gap: waiting for decay, `MEMORY PURGE`, or enabling `activedefrag`?
blocks.reveal: **activedefrag.** Purging (or waiting for decay) can only return the 0.4 GiB of unused pages. The 1.2 GiB sits on pages that still hold live values, and only moving those values onto fewer pages frees them. That is what active defragmentation does.

blocks.md: **Redis active defragmentation** (added in Redis 4.0) is the classic relocation fix. When fragmentation passes a threshold, Redis creates new copies of values in better places, using jemalloc features to tell whether an allocation is causing fragmentation, then frees the old copies, incrementally across all keys. Redis can do this because it knows every pointer to its values. Defaults in `redis.conf`: off (`activedefrag no`), ignore waste below 100 MB, start at 10% fragmentation, full effort at 100%, using 1% to 25% of CPU. It requires Redis's bundled jemalloc, the default on Linux builds.

General C and C++ programs cannot move objects, since any pointer could refer to them. **Mesh** (Powers, Tench, Berger and McGregor, 2019) compacts without relocation. If two pages of the same size class have live objects at **non-overlapping offsets**, Mesh copies one page's objects into the other page at the same offsets, points both virtual pages at that one physical page, and returns the other physical page. Every pointer stays valid. Randomized placement within pages makes non-overlapping pairs likely, and the paper reports memory reductions of 16% for Firefox and 39% for Redis.

scenes.caption: Page A has live objects at slots 0, 3, 5; page B at 1 and 6. Two physical pages hold 5 objects: 5 of 16 slots used (31.25%).
No slot is live in both pages, so they can mesh. B's objects are copied into P1 at the same offsets (1 and 6).
Virtual page B is remapped to P1 and P2 goes back to the OS. Addresses never changed. 5 objects now use 8 slots of physical memory (62.5%).

blocks.md: The kernel has the same problem one level down. Linux's buddy allocator hands out physical blocks of $2^{\text{order}}$ pages, and `/proc/buddyinfo` lists the free blocks of each order per zone. The proc docs call it a useful tool for diagnosing external fragmentation: it shows how big an area you can safely allocate. A 2 MiB huge page needs an order-9 block, which can be missing even when hundreds of MiB are free.

blocks.title: Free blocks per order in one zone (illustrative buddyinfo)

scenes.caption: Free memory = sum of count x 2^order pages = 65,796 pages = 257 MiB, in 37,985 free blocks.
The largest free block is order 6 (256 KiB). An order-9 request (2 MiB) fails despite 257 MiB free: external fragmentation in physical memory.

blocks.caption: The fragmentation index from mm/vmstat.c for order o = 9, with P free pages and B free blocks (the kernel computes it in integer thousandths: 997).

blocks.md: Near 0 the failure is a lack of memory; near 1 it is fragmentation. The `extfrag_threshold` sysctl (default 500) uses this: the kernel will not compact a zone whose index is at or below the threshold and reclaims instead. Here 997 says compaction, which moves pages to rebuild contiguous blocks. To make that possible, the kernel groups pages by mobility into page blocks (2 MiB on x86-64), so movable pages are not scattered among unmovable kernel pages. `compaction_proactiveness` (default 20) also compacts in the background.

Fix the layer the numbers point at. Slack inside pages (active over allocated) needs objects moved or lifetimes grouped. Unused resident pages (resident over active) need purging or decay. Missing high-order physical blocks need compaction. Reaching for the wrong tool spends CPU and changes nothing.

blocks.question: A Redis instance reports mem_fragmentation_ratio 2.1, with used_memory 40 MB and RSS 84 MB. What should you do?
options: Probably nothing: 44 MB of absolute overhead is small and includes code and libraries
Enable activedefrag immediately
Restart the instance to reset fragmentation
Lower dirty_decay_ms to 0
blocks.explain: The Redis docs warn that a high ratio with only a few megabytes of difference is not an issue: the ratio also counts code, shared libraries and stacks, which dominate a small instance. Check allocator_frag_bytes before acting.

blocks.question: Why can Mesh return memory from a C++ program without updating any pointers?
options: It copies objects to new addresses and patches pointers found by scanning the stack
It only frees pages that have no live objects
It merges two physical pages whose live objects sit at different offsets and maps both virtual pages to one
It relies on the kernel's compaction to move pages
blocks.explain: Objects keep their virtual addresses and offsets. Only the virtual-to-physical mapping changes: two virtual pages share one physical page whose slots now hold both sets of objects. Scanning for pointers is impossible in C/C++ because pointers can be hidden or disguised.

blocks.question: A host has 30 GiB free, but 2 MiB transparent huge page allocations keep falling back, and the order-9 fragmentation index is 980. Which statement is right?
options: The host is out of memory; add RAM
The free memory is scattered in small blocks; compaction, not reclaim, is the useful response
Raising extfrag_threshold to 990 will make compaction run more often
buddyinfo will show many free order-9 blocks
blocks.explain: An index near 1000 means the request fails because of fragmentation, not a lack of memory. The kernel compacts only when the index is above extfrag_threshold, so raising the threshold to 990 would suppress compaction here. If order-9 blocks were free, the index would not apply (the request would succeed).
